hints: Focus on what makes a carbon chiral, an sp3 carbon joined to four completely different groups.
Quickly rule out carbons that can never be chiral here, the C=O carbon, the two C=C carbons, all CH2 groups and the two CH3 groups.
Check each remaining ring-junction CH or C-CH3 and the CH-OH carbon one by one for four different attachments to get the final total.
walkthrough:
**Recall the test for a chiral centre**

A chiral centre is a tetrahedral sp3 carbon with four different atoms or groups attached. No plane of symmetry through that carbon.

Rule to apply:
$$\text{chiral C} = \text{sp}^3 \text{ carbon with 4 different groups}$$

**Cross out carbons that cannot be chiral**

Look at the testosterone skeleton. It has four fused rings.

You can immediately ignore the $C=O$ carbon (only 3 attachments), the two $C=C$ carbons in ring A (planar, only 3 attachments), every $CH_2$ group (two H atoms, so not four different groups) and the two $CH_3$ methyl groups (three H atoms).

**Test the carbons that are left**

The only candidates left are the ring-junction carbons and the carbon bearing $OH$.

Going around the steroid framework, there are six such sp3 carbons: the $CH-OH$ carbon, the quaternary $C-CH_3$ carbon next to it, three $CH$ carbons at the junctions of the middle rings, and the quaternary $C-CH_3$ carbon joining ring A to the middle. Each one is joined to four different ring fragments, H or $CH_3$ or $OH$, so each one is chiral.

That gives 6 chiral centres in total.

options.A: 5 is one too few. This usually happens if you miss one of the two quaternary C-CH3 junction carbons, thinking a carbon with no hydrogen cannot be chiral. It can, as long as it has four different carbon groups.
options.B: 6 is correct. After removing C=O, C=C and all CH2 and CH3 carbons, six sp3 carbons remain, each with four different groups: the CH(OH), the two C-CH3 bridgeheads and three CH ring junctions.
options.C: 7 is too many. This usually happens if you count one of the C=C carbons in the left-hand ring as chiral. Alkene carbons are planar sp2 with only three groups, so they can never be chiral centres.
options.D: 8 is too many. This usually happens if you count both alkene carbons or the carbonyl carbon as well as the true six. Only sp3 carbons with four single bonds can be chiral.
